title: Latency-tiered adaptive backoff, session-scoped id-key convention, and retry taxonomy for cross-SDKs
creator: Avery Chen
description: Background: Customers report tricky edge cases with retries and streaming resume: either clients over-retry (cost + duplicate outputs) or under-retry (transient failures cause UX break), and SDK defaults are drifted across languages. Existing guidance is fragmented. Goal: define a single cross-SDK design that provides safe, ergonomic defaults for retries + backoff and a clear idempotency / resume key convention that minimizes duplicates for normal RPCs and streaming generation. This ticket covers the default policy, an adaptive 'latency-tiered' backoff mode, an explicit session-scoped id-key convention for streaming and chunked requests, and a retryable error taxonomy that maps to platform signals (HTTP/gRPC codes, model OOM, rate-limit, capacity fallback). Non-goals: changing server-side semantics or adding new server-only error codes. Success metrics: 1) Reduce customer-observed duplicate-generation incidents by >=50% for streaming recovery scenarios; 2) Reduce billed token increase from client retries on transient 5xx by <=10%; 3) Track and expose retry budget usage per SDK in console and increase signal-to-noise for ops alerts.
proposed_solution: 1) Backoff profiles: introduce three built-in profiles: 'conservative' (longer base/backoff for OLTP, used by default for non-interactive bulk endpoints), 'latency-tiered' (adaptive; automatic profile that measures p50/p95 and selects backoff multipliers and jitter windows at runtime), and 'aggressive' (shorter initial delays, for interactive UIs where duplicate outputs are low-risk). 2) Latency-tiered algorithm: SDK measures a small rolling window of request latencies per route (first 100 requests or 30s warmup), computes p50/p95, selects a base_delay = clamp(p50*0.2, 50ms, 250ms) and max_delay = clamp(p95*0.75, 200ms, 3s). Backoff uses exponential backoff with adaptive multiplier derived from base->max range and capped retry budget per-request (configurable, default 2 retries for generation endpoints, 1 for embeddings). 3) Token-cost-aware retry budgets: optionally reduce retry allowance when the estimated token-cost of a call exceeds configured threshold. 4) Session-scoped id-key convention: for one-shot requests, idempotency key = sha256(user-supplied-id || route || normalized-payload). For streaming/resumable generation, id-key semantics become session-scoped: session_id = client-generated UUID v4 per conversation; per-chunk resume token = HMAC(session_id || sequence_number || model-version) signed with SDK-local key. SDKs expose utility helpers: generate_session_id(), mk_resume_token(session_id, seq), and a high-level resume handler that verifies continuity. 5) Retryable error taxonomy: map server/transport signals to client classification (transient/retryable, throttling/retry-after, non-retryable). E.g., retryable: HTTP 502/503/504, gRPC UNAVAILABLE/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (when server includes retry-info), model-oom transient responses; throttling: HTTP 429 with Retry-After or quota errors (allow 1 retry when Retry-After is <= 5s), non-retryable: 4xx client errors (400/401/403/404), model-validation errors. 6) Streaming resume: prefer resume tokens over naive replays: on transient network disconnect, SDK attempts resume with last-seen seq token; server will accept resume if KV cache still valid; fallback strategy: if resume fails, fall back to a short replay window (replay last N tokens) and only if id-key indicates idempotent/resumable mode. 7) Telemetry: emit retry_attempt, retry_reason, retry_profile, id_key_used, resume_attempt, resume_success as structured metrics and attach to request traces. 8) Migration: keep current default but provide opt-in via setRetryProfile('latency-tiered') and plan staged rollout across languages.
language_ergonomics_examples:
Python example (pattern):
- generate session id: session_id = rw_sdk.util.generate_session_id()
- start streaming: stream = client.chat.stream(model='redwood-...')
- on disconnect: token = rw_sdk.util.mk_resume_token(session_id, last_seq); client.chat.resume(stream_id, token)

TypeScript example (pattern):
- const session = redwood.util.generateSessionId();
- await client.chat.stream({ model: '...' , sessionId: session });
- on 'close' attempt resume: const token = redwood.util.mkResumeToken(session, seq); await client.chat.resume(streamId, token);

Go example (pattern):
- session := redwood.NewSession()
- stream, err := client.StreamChat(ctx, &pb.StreamRequest{SessionId: session.ID})
- on reconnect: tok := redwood.MkResumeToken(session.ID, seq); client.ResumeStream(ctx, stream.Id, tok)
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (opt-in): release helper and config APIs in Python/TS/Go SDKs behind feature flag, ship docs and migration examples (2 weeks). Phase 2 (beta telemetry): enable telemetry for early customers and internal e2e tests (3 weeks). Phase 3 (default flip): depending on telemetry and customer feedback, flip 'latency-tiered' as default for chat/generation endpoints with opt-out knob (4 weeks). Rollback path: immediate opt-out and revert to 'conservative' profile; ensure server-side resume still accepted with older token formats for 90 days.
telemetry_and_metrics: Emit per-request fields: retry_profile, retry_attempts, retry_outcome (succeeded/failed/exhausted), retry_reason (e.g., 503, rate-limit), id_key_type (session|one-shot), resume_attempt, resume_outcome. Add a console dashboard: 'SDK retry budget utilization' with histograms by SDK/lang and route, and an alert when retry budget consumption increases >3x baseline.
compatibility_and_migration: Backwards compatibility: one-shot id keys are compatible with current idempotency ledger. Session resume tokens are additive and will be accepted by servers that have resume-capable KV caches; if resume is unavailable server-side, SDK must degrade to replay-without-duplicate-safety described above. Breaking changes: none planned. Recommend adding flag 'reject-unknown-resume-token' for enterprise customers that want strict guarantees.
qa_and_validation: Unit tests: deterministic id-key generation across languages, token signing/verification tests. Integration tests: simulated transient failures (tcp kill, 503s) to validate resume succeeds and no duplicate messages are delivered in normal flow. Load test: measure additional cost from policy under high 5xx spike and ensure retry budget caps prevent runaway costs. Canary: ship to 5% production traffic for 2 weeks, monitor console metrics and SLO impact.
